topics.title: Array
topics.plain: A row of labeled boxes. Each box holds one value, and each has a number (index) starting at 0.
topics.analogy: Mailboxes in an apartment building — each has a number, walk straight to #5 without checking 1–4.

lessons.title: What is an array? (Start here)
lessons.body: Imagine you're keeping scores for 5 players. You could make 5 separate variables: score1, score2... Or you could put them all in one named list — that's an array. Every slot has a number called an index, starting at 0 (not 1!). You can instantly jump to any slot by its number.

lessons.title: Why reading is instant but inserting at the start is slow
lessons.body: An array reserves one continuous block of memory. To find item [i], the computer does one math calculation: start + i × size. That's why reading is O(1) — instant, regardless of size. But inserting at position 0 forces every existing item to shuffle one spot right. 1 million items = 1 million moves = O(n).
lessons.example:
// Reading: ONE calculation, instant
arr = [5, 9, 2, 7]   stored at addresses 1000, 1004, 1008, 1012
arr[2] → 1000 + 2×4 = address 1008 → value 2  ✓ O(1)

// Inserting at index 0: everyone shifts right
Before: [10, 20, 30, 40]
Insert 5 at front:
  40→slot5, 30→slot4, 20→slot3, 10→slot2  (4 moves)
  place 5→slot1
After:  [5, 10, 20, 30, 40]              O(n) — slow!

lessons.title: Pattern: Two Pointers — turn O(n²) into O(n)
lessons.body: Many array problems naively need two nested loops (O(n²)). The two-pointer trick uses two index variables — one starting at the left, one at the right — moving toward each other. Each step eliminates candidates, giving O(n) total. Works beautifully on sorted arrays.

topics.code:
const arr = [10,20,30];
arr.push(40);        // [10,20,30,40]

deepLessons.title: Cache locality — why arrays are faster than linked lists for reads
deepLessons.body: Array elements live in one continuous block of memory. When you access arr[0], the CPU fetches an entire cache line (~64 bytes = 16 ints). arr[1]…arr[15] are already hot in cache. A linked list node-hop is a random memory address — a cache miss every time.
deepLessons.example:
arr = [5, 9, 2, 7, 3, 8, 1, 6]
Access arr[0]: CPU loads bytes 0-63 into cache.
arr[1] through arr[15] = FREE (already in cache).
Linked list: node0.next → random address → cache miss → +100 cycles penalty.

deepLessons.title: Kadane's Algorithm — Max Subarray in O(n)
deepLessons.body: Track a running sum. At each element, decide: is it better to extend the current subarray, or start fresh? The key insight: if the running sum goes negative, reset it — a negative prefix can only hurt any future subarray.

topics.title: Linked List
topics.plain: A chain of nodes; each node holds a value and a pointer to the next. No random access.
topics.analogy: A treasure hunt — each clue points to the next. To reach clue 5, follow 1→2→3→4.

lessons.title: What is a Linked List? (Start here)
lessons.body: An array stores items side-by-side in memory like seats in a row. A linked list is different — each item can live anywhere in memory, and it holds the address of where the next item is. Think of it like a scavenger hunt: each clue tells you where the next clue is hidden. To reach item #5, you must follow the chain from #1.

lessons.title: Building a node and traversing the chain
lessons.body: A node is just an object with two properties: value (the data) and next (pointer to the next node). The last node points to null — that's how you know you've reached the end. To read item #3, you must walk from the head: node→node→node. That's why reading is O(n), not O(1) like an array.

lessons.title: Pattern: Fast & Slow Pointers — find cycles and midpoints
lessons.body: Use two pointers: slow moves 1 step, fast moves 2 steps. If there's a loop, fast will lap slow and they'll meet. If the list ends normally, fast hits null. When fast reaches the end, slow is at the exact middle — no counting needed.

topics.title: Stack (LIFO)
topics.plain: Last In, First Out. Only add to the top and remove from the top.
topics.analogy: A stack of plates. You grab the top one — never pull from the middle.

lessons.title: What is a Stack? (Start here)
lessons.body: A stack follows one simple rule: the last thing you put in is the first thing you take out (LIFO — Last In, First Out). Picture a stack of dinner plates. You always add a plate to the top, and you always take a plate from the top. You never reach into the middle. In code, you only need two actions: push (add to top) and pop (remove from top).
lessons.example:
const stack = [];

stack.push('plate 1');  // add to top
stack.push('plate 2');  // add to top
stack.push('plate 3');  // add to top

console.log(stack);     // ['plate 1', 'plate 2', 'plate 3']

const top = stack.pop();        // removes 'plate 3'
console.log(top);               // 'plate 3'  ← last in, first out!
console.log(stack);             // ['plate 1', 'plate 2']

lessons.title: Real example: Balanced brackets checker
lessons.body: When you see an opening bracket — push it. When you see a closing bracket — pop from the stack and check if it matches. If the stack is empty at the end, all brackets were balanced. This is one of the most common stack interview questions.

lessons.title: Monotonic Stack — Next Greater Element in O(n)
lessons.body: A monotonic stack keeps elements in increasing or decreasing order by popping when the order is violated. When you find an element larger than the stack's top, you've found the 'next greater element' for everything you pop. Each element is pushed and popped at most once — total O(n).

topics.title: Queue (FIFO)
topics.plain: First In, First Out. Add at back, remove from front.
topics.analogy: A coffee shop line. First to arrive, first served.

lessons.title: What is a Queue? (Start here)
lessons.body: A queue is the opposite of a stack. The first thing you put in is the first thing you take out (FIFO — First In, First Out). Think of a coffee shop line: the person who arrived first gets served first. You join at the back, leave from the front. No cutting in line! In code: enqueue = join the back, dequeue = leave from the front.

lessons.title: Why queues power BFS — finding shortest paths
lessons.body: BFS (Breadth-First Search) uses a queue to explore a graph or tree level by level. You start with the root, put its children in the queue, then process each child and put their children in the queue. The queue guarantees you explore everything at distance 1 before anything at distance 2 — so the first time you reach a target, it's via the shortest path.

lessons.title: Multi-source BFS — start from ALL sources at once
lessons.body: Sometimes you need to find the distance from multiple starting points simultaneously (e.g., nearest gate to each room, nearest rotten orange). Pre-load ALL source nodes into the queue at distance 0 before the loop starts. The wave expands from everywhere at once, guaranteeing each cell gets the minimum distance to any source.

deepLessons.title: Why BFS guarantees shortest path
deepLessons.body: BFS explores nodes in non-decreasing order of distance from the source. The first time you reach the target, you've taken the fewest hops possible. This holds for unweighted graphs — for weighted graphs, use Dijkstra instead.
deepLessons.example:
Graph: A-B(1 hop), A-C(1 hop), B-D(2 hops), C-D(2 hops)
BFS from A:
Q=[A,0]
pop A → enqueue B(1), C(1)
pop B → enqueue D(2)
pop C → D already queued
pop D → FOUND at distance 2
Guaranteed shortest: can't reach D in < 2 hops.

topics.title: Hash Table
topics.plain: Magic dictionary. Key → value, instantly.
topics.analogy: A library with barcodes. Scan → know the exact shelf.

lessons.title: What is a Hash Table? (Start here)
lessons.body: A hash table is like a magic dictionary. You give it a word (the key), and it instantly gives you back the definition (the value). No scanning from the start — it jumps straight to the answer. In JavaScript, plain objects {} and Map() are both hash tables. This is the single most useful data structure for solving interview problems.

lessons.title: How it works: hash functions and collisions
lessons.body: Under the hood, a hash function converts your key into a slot number (an index into an array). The same key always gives the same slot. If two different keys accidentally map to the same slot (a collision), it stores them as a small chain. With a good hash function, chains stay tiny, keeping lookups close to O(1).

lessons.title: Pattern: Two Sum — the one-pass hash map trick
lessons.body: For each number, calculate the complement you need (target - current). Check if that complement is already in the map. If yes, you're done. If no, store the current number. This pattern extends to hundreds of 'pair/group' problems — it's the single most important hash table pattern to know.

topics.title: Binary Search Tree
topics.plain: Each node up to 2 children. Smaller left, larger right. Search halves the problem each step.
topics.analogy: Guessing game: higher or lower than 50? Each answer eliminates half.

lessons.title: What is a Tree? (Start here)
lessons.body: A tree organises data in a parent-child hierarchy. There's one root at the top, and each node can have children below it. Nodes with no children are called leaves. Your computer's file system is a tree — folders contain sub-folders. A Binary Search Tree adds a special rule: everything in the left subtree is smaller than the current node, and everything in the right is larger.

lessons.title: Search and Insert both walk down in O(log n)
lessons.body: Because of the left/right rule, every comparison eliminates half the remaining nodes. This is like the 'guess a number' game — every 'too high' or 'too low' halves the search. For 1 million nodes, that's only about 20 comparisons! Insert works the same way: walk down until you find an empty spot.

lessons.title: Three traversal orders — in-order gives sorted output
lessons.body: Traversal means visiting every node in a specific order. In-order (Left → Node → Right) visits nodes in sorted order — it's a free sort! Pre-order (Node → Left → Right) is useful for copying a tree. Post-order (Left → Right → Node) is useful for deleting a tree.

lessons.title: Danger: unbalanced trees degrade to O(n)
lessons.body: If you insert values in sorted order (1, 2, 3, 4, 5...), every node goes to the right — you get a linked list disguised as a tree. All operations become O(n). Self-balancing trees (AVL, Red-Black) fix this by automatically rotating after each insert to maintain O(log n).
lessons.example:
// Inserting 1,2,3,4,5 in order — becomes a line:
1
 \
  2
   \
    3
     \
      4  ← height=n, search=O(n), useless!

// AVL tree inserts same values, stays balanced:
    2
   / \
  1   4
     / \
    3   5   ← height=log n, search=O(log n) ✓

topics.title: Heap / Priority Queue
topics.plain: A tree where the parent is always smaller (min-heap) or larger (max-heap) than its children. Top is always the extreme.
topics.analogy: Hospital ER triage — most critical patient always served next, regardless of arrival order.

lessons.title: What is a Heap? (Start here)
lessons.body: Imagine a hospital ER. Patients arrive in random order, but you always need to treat the most critical one next — not the first one who arrived. A heap (or priority queue) solves this: you can insert items in any order, but you always get the smallest (min-heap) or largest (max-heap) back first. It's like a queue, but with priorities instead of arrival order.

lessons.title: Stored as an array — parent/child via index math
lessons.body: A heap looks like a tree but lives in a plain array — no pointers needed. The parent-child relationship is encoded by index: node at index i has its left child at 2i+1 and right child at 2i+2. Its parent is at Math.floor((i-1)/2). This makes it extremely memory-efficient.

lessons.title: Insert (bubble up) and Extract-min (sift down)
lessons.body: To insert: add at the end, then swap with parent until the heap rule is restored ('bubble up'). To extract the minimum: swap root with the last element, remove last, then push the new root down, swapping with the smaller child ('sift down'). Both operations are O(log n).
lessons.example:
// Insert 2 into heap [1, 3, 5, 7, 9]:
append:  [1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 2]
parent of 2 = 5 → 2 < 5 → swap: [1, 3, 2, 7, 9, 5]
parent of 2 = 1 → 2 > 1 → stop ✓

// Extract-min from [1, 3, 2, 7, 9, 5]:
swap root↔last:  [5, 3, 2, 7, 9, 1] → remove 1
sift down 5: smaller child is 2 → swap
[2, 3, 5, 7, 9] ✓  new min=2

lessons.title: Pattern: Top-K and Two-Heap Median
lessons.body: For 'top K largest elements': counter-intuitively, use a MIN-heap of size K. When the heap exceeds K, pop the smallest. At the end, the heap contains the K largest. For running median: maintain two heaps — a max-heap for the lower half and a min-heap for the upper half. The median is always at one of the tops.

topics.title: Graph
topics.plain: Nodes (vertices) connected by edges. Edges can be directed/undirected, weighted/unweighted.
topics.analogy: A social network. People are nodes, friendships are edges. Paths = chains of introductions.

lessons.title: What is a Graph? (Start here)
lessons.body: A graph is just a bunch of nodes (also called vertices) connected by lines (edges). Unlike a tree, there's no fixed parent-child relationship — any node can connect to any other. Think of a social network: people are nodes, friendships are edges. Or a road map: cities are nodes, roads are edges. Edges can be one-way (directed) or two-way (undirected), and can carry weights like distance or cost.

lessons.title: Two ways to store a graph: list vs matrix
lessons.body: Adjacency list (a map from node → list of neighbors) is compact and great when most nodes have only a few neighbors. Adjacency matrix is a 2D grid where matrix[i][j]=1 means there's an edge — fast for 'is there an edge between i and j?' but uses O(V²) memory even for sparse graphs.

lessons.title: BFS finds the shortest path in an unweighted graph
lessons.body: Breadth-First Search uses a queue to explore level by level. Start with the source, mark it as visited at distance 0. Pop the next node, look at its neighbors — they're at distance+1. The first time you reach the target, BFS guarantees that's the minimum number of edges (shortest path) for unweighted graphs.

lessons.title: Dijkstra — shortest path with weighted edges
lessons.body: When edges have weights (distances, costs), BFS doesn't work. Dijkstra uses a min-heap (priority queue) of (distance, node) pairs. Always pop the closest unvisited node, then 'relax' its neighbors — if going through it gives a shorter total, update their distances. It's BFS with priorities.

deepLessons.title: Kahn's Algorithm for Topological Sort
deepLessons.body: Compute in-degree of every node. Put all nodes with in-degree 0 in a queue. Repeatedly pop a node, add it to the result, and decrement its neighbors' in-degrees — enqueue any that reach 0. If result length < N, a cycle exists.

indegree: [0,1,1,2]
queue: [0]
pop 0 → result=[0]; decrement 1,2 → indegree=[0,0,0,2]
enqueue 1,2; pop 1 → result=[0,1]; decrement 3 → indegree[3]=1
pop 2 → result=[0,1,2]; decrement 3 → indegree[3]=0; enqueue 3
pop 3 → result=[0,1,2,3]  (no cycle — length=4=N ✓)

topics.plain: A tree where each edge is a character. Walking from root spells a prefix. O(L) insert & lookup, where L is word length.
topics.analogy: A phone-book index arranged by letter. 'ca-' then 't', 'r', 'b' fan out from 'ca'.

lessons.title: What is a Trie? (Start here)
lessons.body: Imagine you're building autocomplete for a search bar. Someone types 'ca' and you need to instantly suggest cat, car, care, cart. Searching a list one-by-one would be slow. A Trie (pronounced 'try') solves this: it's a tree where each edge is a single character. Words that share a prefix share the same path. Following 'c' → 'a' lands you at a node where every word in the subtree starts with 'ca'.

lessons.title: Node structure and the insert/search logic
lessons.body: Each node holds a children map (character → next node) and a flag (isEnd) marking whether a word ends here. To insert: walk character by character, creating nodes as needed. To search: walk character by character, return false if any step fails. The flag matters — 'ca' might be a prefix but not actually a word.

lessons.title: Pattern: Autocomplete via DFS from prefix node
lessons.body: To return all words starting with a prefix: walk to the prefix node, then DFS down to collect every node marked as a word ending. This is how Google's search box works under the hood. For grid problems like Word Search II, putting the dictionary into a trie lets you prune entire DFS branches when no word in the dictionary continues with the current path.

topics.title: Set
topics.plain: Collection of unique items with O(1) add, remove, has. Order-less.
topics.analogy: A bag of unique stamps — duplicates are silently ignored.

lessons.title: What is a Set? (Start here)
lessons.body: A Set is a collection that automatically refuses duplicates. Add 'apple' twice — it only keeps one. It's the perfect tool for answering 'have I seen this before?' questions. Under the hood it's a hash table that only stores keys (no values), so all operations — add, has, delete — are O(1) average.

lessons.title: Set operations: union, intersection, difference
lessons.body: Sets support the classic math operations. Union (A ∪ B) — everything in either. Intersection (A ∩ B) — only what's in both. Difference (A \ B) — what's in A but not B. JavaScript doesn't have built-in operators for these, but they're easy to write in a few lines.

lessons.body: Given an unsorted array of integers, find the longest run of consecutive numbers. Sorting is O(n log n). With a Set, you can do it in O(n). The trick: only start counting from a 'sequence start' — a number n where n-1 is NOT in the set. This ensures each number is visited at most twice total.

deepLessons.body: Naive sort is O(n log n). With a Set, you can do O(n): build a Set of all numbers, then only start counting from 'sequence heads' — numbers where (n-1) is NOT in the set. This ensures each number is visited at most twice.

nums = [100, 4, 200, 1, 3, 2]
set = {100,4,200,1,3,2}

Check 100: set.has(99)? No → start counting. 101? No → length=1.
Check 4:   set.has(3)?  Yes → skip (not a head).
Check 1:   set.has(0)?  No → count: 1,2,3,4 → length=4 ✓
Answer: 4    Time: O(n) — each element counted once.

topics.title: Binary Search
topics.plain: Find a value in a sorted array by repeatedly halving the search range.
topics.analogy: Guessing a number 1–100: always guess the middle. In 7 guesses you find any number up to 128.

lessons.title: What is Binary Search? The number guessing game
lessons.body: Pretend a friend is thinking of a number from 1 to 100. Instead of guessing 1, 2, 3... you guess the MIDDLE — 50. They say 'higher' or 'lower', and you've just eliminated half the possibilities in one step. Repeat. In 7 guesses you can find any number up to 128. That's binary search. The catch: it only works on SORTED data — without order, 'higher' and 'lower' have no meaning.

lessons.title: The core loop — track lo, hi, and mid
lessons.body: Keep two pointers: lo (lowest possible index) and hi (highest possible index). Each iteration, compute mid = (lo+hi)/2 and compare arr[mid] to your target. Move lo up or hi down to narrow the range. Watch out for off-by-one: pick whether hi is inclusive (use lo<=hi, hi=mid-1) or exclusive (use lo<hi, hi=mid) and stick with it consistently.

lessons.title: Pattern: Binary Search the ANSWER (most powerful trick)
lessons.body: Binary search isn't just for arrays! If your problem has a monotonic 'yes/no' check — meaning if x works, every value larger than x also works — you can binary search the answer space directly. Examples: 'min days to ship packages of capacity C', 'min eating speed to finish bananas in H hours'. This unlocks problems that look unrelated to sorted arrays.

easy.body: Index where target should go in a sorted array.
easy.hint: Return lo at the end of standard BS.

easy.title: Binary Search
easy.body: Return the index of target in a sorted array, or -1.
easy.hint: Standard lo/hi loop on the sorted range.
easy.solution: while(lo<=hi){ const m=(lo+hi)>>1; if(a[m]===t) return m; a[m]<t?lo=m+1:hi=m-1; } return -1;

easy.body: Integer square root (floor) of x.
easy.hint: Binary search m where m*m ≤ x.
easy.solution: while(lo<=hi){ const m=(lo+hi)>>1; if(m*m<=x){ ans=m; lo=m+1; } else hi=m-1; } return ans;

easy.body: Find the first bad version with minimal API calls.

upperBound: find first i with arr[i]>target

medium.body: Search a target in a rotated sorted array in O(log n).
medium.hint: One half is always sorted — decide which, then narrow.

if(a[lo]<=a[m]){ if(a[lo]<=t&&t<a[m]) hi=m-1; else lo=m+1; }
else { if(a[m]<t&&t<=a[hi]) lo=m+1; else hi=m-1; }

medium.hint: Move toward the larger neighbor.
medium.solution: while(lo<hi){ const m=(lo+hi)>>1; a[m]<a[m+1]?lo=m+1:hi=m; } return lo;

Need: A[i-1]<=B[j] and B[j-1]<=A[i]

quiz.why: You need order so halving the range makes sense.

git bisect: finds the first bad commit by binary-searching the commit history.
numpy.searchsorted: O(log n) insertion point in sorted arrays.
Load balancer autoscaling: binary search on 'minimum capacity to handle N requests/sec'.

deepLessons.body: Many problems have a monotonic check function: 'is capacity C sufficient?' True for all C ≥ answer, false for all C < answer. Binary search C directly — no array needed. Works for: ship packages in D days, koko eating bananas, minimum days to bloom flowers.

topics.title: Sorting Algorithms
topics.plain: Arrange items in order. The workhorses: merge sort (stable, O(n log n)), quick sort (in-place, usually fastest), and simple O(n²) ones.
topics.analogy: Sorting a deck of cards: merge sort = split into halves, sort each, interleave. Quick sort = pick a card, split into smaller/larger piles, repeat.

lessons.title: What is Sorting? Why bother?
lessons.body: Sorting puts items in order — smallest to largest, A to Z, oldest to newest. Why? Because once data is sorted, MANY other operations get dramatically faster: binary search becomes possible, finding duplicates is trivial, and median/min/max are obvious. In practice, you almost always use the language's built-in sort. Just remember to always pass a comparator for numbers in JS!

lessons.title: Insertion Sort — simple, perfect for small arrays
lessons.body: How you'd sort cards in your hand. Pick up cards one at a time, slide each into its correct position among the cards you've already arranged. It's O(n²) in the worst case, but blazingly fast on small or nearly-sorted arrays — that's why most language sort implementations use it as a fallback below ~10 items.

lessons.title: Merge Sort — divide and conquer in O(n log n)
lessons.body: Split the array in half. Recursively sort each half. Then merge the two sorted halves into one sorted array — that merge step is O(n) because you just compare front elements and pick the smaller. The recursion is log n deep, each level costs O(n), so total is O(n log n). Stable (preserves order of equals) and predictable, but needs O(n) extra space.

lessons.title: Quick Sort and when to use Counting/Radix
lessons.body: Quick Sort picks a 'pivot' and partitions everything smaller to its left, larger to its right. Recurse on both sides. Average O(n log n), worst O(n²) on bad pivot. In-place, so cache-friendly. Counting/Radix sort skip comparisons entirely — they distribute items into buckets — and run in O(n) when values are integers in a small range.

deepLessons.body: During the merge step, when you take an element from the RIGHT sub-array before the left is exhausted, every remaining element in the left sub-array forms an inversion with it. This counts all inversions in O(n log n) — much better than O(n²) brute force.
deepLessons.example:
arr = [3, 1, 2]  → 2 inversions: (3,1) and (3,2)

Merge [3] and [1,2]:
Compare 3 vs 1 → take 1 (from right).
Left has [3] remaining → 1 inversion.
Compare 3 vs 2 → take 2 (from right).
Left has [3] remaining → 1 inversion.
Total = 2 ✓

topics.title: Recursion
topics.plain: A function that calls itself on a smaller version of the same problem until a base case stops it.
topics.analogy: Russian nesting dolls — to solve the big doll, open it and solve the smaller one, and so on until you can't.

lessons.title: What is Recursion? A function that calls itself
lessons.body: Recursion is when a function solves a problem by calling itself on a smaller version of the same problem. Sounds wild, but it's natural. Think of Russian nesting dolls: to count them all, open the outer one and count the inner one (which is itself a smaller nesting-doll problem). The two non-negotiable parts: a BASE CASE (when to stop) and a RECURSIVE CASE (how to shrink). Forget the base case → infinite loop → crash.

lessons.title: The call stack — every call waits for the next
lessons.body: When a function calls itself, the current call's state is paused and pushed onto the call stack. The new call runs to completion, returns its value, and then the paused call resumes with that value. Too deep recursion = stack overflow crash. JavaScript typically allows ~10,000 nested calls before crashing. For very deep recursion, convert to iteration with an explicit stack.
lessons.example:
factorial(3)            // pushed onto stack
└─ factorial(2)         // pushed, waits
   └─ factorial(1)      // pushed, waits
      └─ returns 1      // base case — pops
   returns 2 × 1 = 2    // pops
returns 3 × 2 = 6       // pops, done!

// Visual: each indent level = one stack frame waiting.
// 1000+ levels in JavaScript → RangeError: Maximum call stack

lessons.title: Trust the Recursion — the expert mental model
lessons.body: Don't trace every call in your head — that's a quick way to get lost. Instead: (1) precisely DEFINE what your function returns. (2) ASSUME it works correctly for smaller inputs. (3) Use that assumption to solve the current case. This 'trust the recursion' mindset is the difference between hating recursion and loving it.

useNo: Very deep recursion without tail calls

deepLessons.title: Trust the Recursion — the most important mental model
deepLessons.body: Don't trace every call stack mentally. Instead: (1) define precisely what your function returns, (2) assume it works correctly on strictly smaller inputs, (3) use that assumption to solve the current case. This is how experts write recursive code.
deepLessons.example:
Problem: max depth of a binary tree.
Definition: depth(node) = height of the subtree rooted at node.
Assume: depth(node.left) and depth(node.right) work correctly.
Combine: return 1 + Math.max(depth(left), depth(right)).
Base case: depth(null) = 0.

Don't trace the whole tree — trust the assumption and combine.

topics.title: BFS & DFS
topics.plain: Two ways to walk a graph or tree. BFS uses a queue (level by level). DFS uses a stack or recursion (deep first).
topics.analogy: BFS = ripples in a pond — spreading out evenly. DFS = diving head-first into a cave, backtracking only when stuck.

lessons.title: BFS vs DFS — Two ways to explore
lessons.body: When you need to visit every node in a tree or graph, you have two strategies. BFS (Breadth-First Search) goes WIDE — visit all immediate neighbors, then their neighbors, etc. Like ripples spreading out from a stone in a pond. DFS (Depth-First Search) goes DEEP — pick one path and follow it as far as you can before backtracking. Like exploring a cave by diving down each tunnel completely before trying the next.

lessons.title: BFS template — when you need shortest path
lessons.body: Use BFS when the question involves 'shortest path', 'minimum hops', or 'fewest steps' on an unweighted graph. The queue guarantees you finish all nodes at distance d before any at distance d+1, so the first time you reach the target, it's via the minimum number of edges.

lessons.title: DFS template — recursion is most natural
lessons.body: Use DFS when you need to explore all paths, detect cycles, do topological sort, or count connected components. Recursion is usually the cleanest implementation — the call stack acts as your DFS stack automatically.

lessons.title: Choosing the right traversal — quick decision rules
lessons.body: Need shortest path on UNWEIGHTED graph → BFS. Need shortest path on WEIGHTED graph → Dijkstra (NOT BFS). Need to enumerate all paths or detect cycles → DFS. Topological sort → DFS or Kahn's BFS. Counting components or flood fill → either works (DFS is shorter to write).

useYes: DFS: cycle detect, topo sort, components

topics.title: Dynamic Programming
topics.plain: Solve problems by breaking them into overlapping subproblems and storing each subproblem's answer so you never recompute it.
topics.analogy: Climbing stairs: to know ways to step #10, you already know ways to step #9 and #8. Remember them so you don't recount.

lessons.title: What is DP? Don't do the same work twice
lessons.body: Dynamic Programming sounds intimidating but it's really one simple idea: don't compute the same thing twice. If you've already calculated fib(5), don't compute it again — store it. This turns exponential O(2^n) recursion into linear O(n). Step 1 is always: write the natural recursive solution. Step 2: notice the recursion is recomputing things. Step 3: cache results. That's it. That's DP.

lessons.title: Top-down (memoization) vs bottom-up (tabulation)
lessons.body: Two flavors of DP. TOP-DOWN: write the recursion + add a cache. Easier to think about. BOTTOM-UP: fill a table starting from the base case, building up to the answer. Often allows tossing the cache and using a few rolling variables (O(1) space). Both have the same time complexity — pick whichever you can write faster.

lessons.title: How to spot a DP problem
lessons.body: Three signals: (1) the problem asks 'count', 'maximize', 'minimize', or 'is it possible'. (2) At each step you make a choice that affects future choices. (3) The naive recursive solution recomputes the same subproblems. If those three are present, DP is your tool.

lessons.title: 2D DP — Edit Distance and grid problems
lessons.body: When subproblems depend on TWO indices (e.g., comparing two strings), use a 2D table. Edit Distance: minimum operations (insert/delete/replace) to turn s into t. dp[i][j] = best for s[0..i] → t[0..j]. The recurrence considers all three operations and picks the minimum.

complexity: Can often shrink with rolling arrays
useNo: Subproblems don't repeat → use plain recursion or greedy

deepLessons.title: DP is Careful Brute Force — the right mental model
deepLessons.body: The naive recursive solution is correct but exponential because it recomputes the same sub-problems. Memoization caches each unique input tuple — turning the exponential call tree into a DAG. If you can write the recursive solution, you can always memoize it.
deepLessons.example:
Naive fib(5) call tree:
           fib(5)
          /      \
       fib(4)   fib(3)
       /   \    /   \
    fib(3) fib(2) fib(2) fib(1)  ← duplicates!

With memo: each fib(k) computed ONCE.
Time: O(n)   Space: O(n) memo or O(1) rolling vars.

topics.title: Two Pointers
topics.plain: Use two indices walking an array — toward each other, or in the same direction — to solve in O(n).
topics.analogy: Two hands running along a ruler — often meeting in the middle or one catching up to the other.

lessons.title: What are Two Pointers? (Start here)
lessons.body: Many array problems naively need two nested loops — that's O(n²). The Two Pointers technique uses two index variables (often called left and right) walking through the array, doing one pass instead of n². The trick: each step makes provable progress, so you visit each element at most a constant number of times. Total: O(n).

lessons.title: Converging pointers — perfect for sorted arrays
lessons.body: Pointers start at opposite ends and move toward each other. Each step, one pointer advances based on a comparison, eliminating one candidate per move. This is THE go-to pattern for pair-sum / triple-sum problems on sorted arrays. The 'sorted' part is critical — it gives you directional certainty.

lessons.title: Same-direction (slow/fast) — in-place filtering
lessons.body: Both pointers start at the left and move right at different speeds. Slow tracks where the next valid element should be written. Fast scans through the array. When fast finds something keepable, write it at slow and bump slow. Perfect for removing duplicates or filtering in-place, all in O(1) extra space.

useNo: Need index-based random access unrelated to order

easy.title: Valid Palindrome
easy.body: Ignoring non-alphanumerics, is the string a palindrome?
easy.hint: Two pointers skipping non-alnum.

easy.body: Find two numbers in a sorted array that sum to target.
easy.hint: Move left up or right down based on the sum.
easy.solution: while(l<r){ const s=a[l]+a[r]; if(s===t) return [l+1,r+1]; s<t?l++:r--; }

for i in 0..n-3:

deepLessons.title: Why sorting enables Two Pointers
deepLessons.body: Sorting gives directional certainty. If left + right < target, moving left forward can only increase (or maintain) the sum. If left + right > target, moving right backward can only decrease it. This monotonicity is what turns O(n²) brute force into O(n).
deepLessons.example:
sorted = [1, 2, 4, 7, 11, 15], target = 15
l=0,r=5: 1+15=16 > 15 → r-- (reduce sum)
l=0,r=4: 1+11=12 < 15 → l++ (increase sum)
l=1,r=4: 2+11=13 < 15 → l++
l=2,r=4: 4+11=15 = 15 → FOUND [2,4]
Each step makes provable progress: O(n) total.

topics.title: Sliding Window
topics.plain: A window [l..r] that grows and shrinks over an array/string to track a running condition — sum, distinct count, etc.
topics.analogy: A magnifying glass scanning a line of text. Expand until condition breaks, shrink until it holds again.

lessons.title: What is a Sliding Window? (Start here)
lessons.body: Many problems ask 'what's the best contiguous subarray/substring of length k?' Naively, you'd compute the sum of every window from scratch — O(n×k). A sliding window is smarter: keep two pointers (left, right) defining the current window. To slide one step right, ADD the new element on the right and SUBTRACT the old element falling off the left. You update incrementally instead of recomputing.

lessons.title: Variable-size window — expand and shrink based on invariant
lessons.body: Sometimes the window size isn't fixed — you grow it while a condition holds and shrink it when violated. Pattern: keep moving right (expand). When the window becomes invalid, move left until it's valid again. Track the best valid window seen so far. Both pointers only move forward, so total work is O(n).

lessons.title: Trigger words — knowing when to reach for it
lessons.body: If you see 'contiguous', 'subarray', 'substring', 'window', or 'k distinct' / 'k characters' in a problem, sliding window is your first guess. The deciding question: can the window state be updated cheaply when you slide? If yes (counts, sums, frequencies), sliding window crushes it in O(n). If you need full-array sorted state, look elsewhere.

Longest substring with ≤ k distinct chars → Variable window (shrink on violation)
Minimum window containing all target chars → Variable window (shrink on valid)
Contiguous subarray matching a condition → Sliding window + state map/counter
interviewTips: Name the variant: fixed-size vs. variable-size (dynamic). They have slightly different templates.
Variable window invariant: expand r always; shrink l while the window is invalid; update best when valid.
State what 'valid' means upfront: 'the window is valid as long as it has ≤ k distinct characters.'
Sliding window is O(n) because both l and r only move forward — 2n steps maximum.
realWorld: TCP congestion control: the send window is a fixed-size sliding window over the byte stream.
Stock market moving averages (SMA, EMA): fixed-size window over price history.
Network traffic analysis: rate limiting is a sliding window over the last N seconds of requests.
Real-time anomaly detection: compare current window statistics against a historical baseline.

deepLessons.title: The Variable Sliding Window Template
deepLessons.body: The two pointers l and r only move right. r expands the window by one each iteration. l shrinks the window (from the left) only when the invariant is violated — and shrinks until the invariant is restored. Track best whenever the window is valid.
deepLessons.example:
Longest substring with at most k=2 distinct chars:
s = 'eceba'
l=0,r=0: {e:1} size=1 ≤ 2 ✓  best=1
l=0,r=1: {e:1,c:1} size=2 ≤ 2 ✓  best=2
l=0,r=2: {e:2,c:1} size=2 ✓  best=3
l=0,r=3: {e:2,c:1,b:1} size=3 > 2 SHRINK
  l=1: {e:1,c:1,b:1} still 3 SHRINK
  l=2: {c:1,b:1} size=2 ✓  best=3
l=2,r=4: {c:1,b:1,a:1} > 2 SHRINK
  → l=3: {b:1,a:1} ✓  best=max(3,2)=3
Answer: 3

topics.title: Backtracking
topics.plain: Build a solution step by step. On failure, undo the last step and try another choice. Brute force with memory.
topics.analogy: Navigating a maze with chalk — mark your path, and if you hit a dead end, erase your last mark and try a different turn.

lessons.title: What is Backtracking? Try-and-undo
lessons.body: Backtracking is how you'd solve a maze: at each junction, try one direction. If you hit a dead end, walk back to the last junction and try a different direction. In code: at each step, pick a choice → recurse → if it didn't work, UNDO the choice and try the next one. The 'undo' step is what makes it 'backtracking' — without it, it's just brute force.

lessons.title: The template — choose, recurse, unchoose
lessons.body: Almost every backtracking problem fits this template. Pair every state mutation with its inverse: push/pop, set/clear, mark/unmark. Forgetting the undo step is the #1 backtracking bug — it leaves stale state that corrupts later attempts.

lessons.title: Pruning — the difference between fast and hopeless
lessons.body: Backtracking is exponential by nature. Pruning means recognizing dead branches EARLY and not recursing into them. For N-Queens: before placing a queen, check that no other queen is in the same column or diagonal — if there is, don't even start that branch. Smart pruning routinely turns 2^n into something completable in milliseconds.

useNo: Search space too large even pruned

easy.hint: At each index, include or skip.

easy.hint: Recurse with a start index; pick increasing values.
easy.solution: dfs(start,cur){ if(cur.length===k){ res.push([...cur]); return; } for(i=start;i<=n;i++){ cur.push(i); dfs(i+1,cur); cur.pop(); } }

quiz.why: Place/undo with constraint pruning is textbook backtracking.

quiz.why: The un-choose (undo) step restores state so sibling branches start clean.

opts: Abandoning a branch as soon as it can't possibly lead to a valid answer
quiz.why: Check constraints BEFORE recursing — N-Queens without pruning is hopeless.

cheatsheet.oneLiner: Try → recurse → undo. Brute force with memory.
cheatsheet.useWhen: Enumerate all valid configurations: subsets, permutations, Sudoku, N-Queens.
cheatsheet.pattern: Choose → recurse → unchoose. Pair every state mutation with its inverse.
cheatsheet.gotcha: Forgetting the undo step leaves stale state — corrupts later branches.

patternCues: Generate ALL valid combinations / permutations / subsets → Backtracking
Constraint satisfaction puzzle (Sudoku, N-Queens) → Backtracking with pruning
Key signal word: 'all possible' or 'every valid' → Backtracking (not DP)
Path in graph visiting all nodes / states → Backtracking with state undo
interviewTips: State the template explicitly: 'choose → recurse → unchoose (undo).'
Pair every state-change with its undo: path.push/pop, used[i]=true/false, board[r][c]=digit/'.'.
For inputs with duplicates: sort first, then skip: if(i > start && arr[i] === arr[i-1]) continue.
Pruning is where you show cleverness — state the pruning condition clearly before coding the loop.
realWorld: SAT solvers (used in chip design verification): backtracking search over boolean variable assignments.
Crossword puzzle generators: backtrack over word placements.
Compiler register allocation: graph coloring via backtracking.
Game AI: minimax search tree (chess, Go) uses backtracking with alpha-beta pruning.

deepLessons.title: Backtracking Template — Choose / Recurse / Unchoose
deepLessons.body: The pattern is always the same: (1) if the current path is a valid complete solution, record it. (2) For each possible next choice, check if it's valid, make it, recurse, then UNDO it. The undo step is the defining characteristic.

topics.title: Greedy
topics.plain: Always take the choice that looks best right now. Works when local optima compose into a global optimum.
topics.analogy: Making change with 25¢, 10¢, 5¢, 1¢ — always grab the biggest coin that fits. Works for U.S. coins; fails for {1, 3, 4} making 6.

lessons.title: What is Greedy? Always take the best NOW
lessons.body: A greedy algorithm makes the choice that looks best at this moment, without thinking about future consequences. Surprisingly, this works for many problems! Example: making change with US coins (25¢, 10¢, 5¢, 1¢) — always grab the largest coin that fits. The big trap: greedy doesn't always work. The hard part isn't writing a greedy solution — it's proving it produces the optimal answer.

lessons.title: Activity Selection — the canonical correct greedy
lessons.body: You have a list of meetings with start/end times. Pick the maximum number that don't overlap. The greedy choice: always pick the meeting that ENDS earliest (not starts earliest). Why? Ending early leaves the most room for future meetings. This 'sort by end time' insight is the heart of many interval problems.

lessons.title: When greedy fails — and the 'exchange argument'
lessons.body: If a future choice can be blocked by your greedy decision, greedy is wrong — typically DP is the fix. To convince an interviewer your greedy works, use an EXCHANGE ARGUMENT: argue that for any optimal solution, you could swap its first choice for the greedy choice without making things worse. If true, the greedy solution must be optimal.

useYes: Problem asks for a single best choice path

easy.hint: Sort both; two pointers.

CPU scheduling (Shortest Job First): greedy minimizes average waiting time.
Dijkstra's algorithm: greedily always relax the nearest unvisited node.

deepLessons.title: Activity Selection — the canonical greedy proof
deepLessons.body: Sort intervals by end time. Greedily pick the activity with the earliest finish that doesn't conflict with the last picked. Proof by exchange: suppose an optimal solution starts with activity A (not the earliest-finishing). We can always swap A for the earliest-finishing B — B ends no later than A, so it conflicts with nothing more, and the rest of the solution is unaffected.
deepLessons.example:
Activities: [(1,4),(3,5),(0,6),(5,7),(3,9),(5,9),(6,10),(8,11),(8,12),(2,14),(12,16)]
Sorted by end: [(1,4),(3,5),(0,6),(5,7),(3,9),(5,9),(6,10),(8,11),(8,12),(2,14),(12,16)]
Greedy picks:
  Pick (1,4) — first, always take earliest finish
  (3,5) conflicts (3<4) skip
  (0,6) conflicts (0<4) skip
  Pick (5,7) — starts at 5 ≥ 4 ✓
  Pick (8,11) — starts at 8 ≥ 7 ✓
  Pick (12,16) — starts at 12 ≥ 11 ✓
Result: 4 activities — optimal.

topics.title: Intervals
topics.plain: Problems about ranges with a start and end (meetings, bookings). Almost always: sort first, then sweep once.
topics.analogy: A wall calendar. To spot double-bookings, you list meetings in start order and look at each pair of neighbours.

lessons.title: What is an interval problem? (Start here)
lessons.body: An interval is just a pair [start, end] — a meeting from 9 to 10, a booking from Tue to Fri. Interview questions ask things like: do any overlap? merge the overlapping ones. how many rooms do I need? The single most important skill: checking whether two intervals overlap. Two intervals overlap when each one starts before the other ends.

lessons.title: The master move: sort by start, then sweep
lessons.body: Unsorted intervals are chaos — any pair might overlap. Sorted by start time, overlaps can only happen between NEIGHBOURS, so one linear sweep answers most questions. Merge Intervals: walk the sorted list; if the current interval starts before the previous one ends, they overlap — extend the previous end. Otherwise start a new group.

lessons.title: Meeting Rooms II — min-heap of end times
lessons.body: 'How many meetings run at the same time?' Sort by start. Keep a min-heap of end times of ongoing meetings. For each new meeting: if the earliest-ending meeting is already over (its end ≤ new start), pop it — that room is free. Push the new end time. The largest the heap ever gets = rooms needed. Same idea solves CPU scheduling and platform-count problems.

easy.title: Meeting Rooms
easy.body: Can one person attend all meetings?
easy.hint: Sort by start; any neighbour overlap → false.
easy.example:
sort by start
for i in 1..n-1:
  if start[i] < end[i-1] → return false
return true

medium.title: Merge Intervals
medium.body: Merge all overlapping intervals.
medium.hint: Sort by start; extend or push.

hard.title: Meeting Rooms II
hard.body: Minimum number of conference rooms required.
hard.hint: Sort by start; min-heap of end times; peak heap size.
hard.example:
sort by start
for each meeting:
  if heap.top <= start: heap.pop()  // room freed
  heap.push(end)
answer = max heap size seen

quiz.why: Sorted by start, overlaps only occur between neighbours — one sweep solves it.

quiz.q: After sorting by start, [s,e] overlaps the previous merged interval when…
quiz.why: It starts before the previous one finishes — extend the end with max(prevEnd, e).

quiz.q: Meeting Rooms II keeps a min-heap of…
quiz.why: The root is the meeting that frees a room soonest; peak heap size = rooms needed.

cheatsheet.oneLiner: Ranges [start, end]: sort by start, sweep once.
cheatsheet.useWhen: Meetings, bookings, merging ranges, 'how many at once' questions.
cheatsheet.pattern: Overlap: aStart < bEnd && bStart < aEnd. Min rooms: min-heap of end times.
cheatsheet.gotcha: Decide whether touching intervals ([1,3],[3,5]) count as overlapping — ask!

topics.title: Union-Find (DSU)
topics.plain: Tracks which items belong to the same group. Two near-O(1) operations: union (merge groups) and find (which group?).
topics.analogy: Friend circles at a party. When two people shake hands their circles merge — and you can instantly ask 'are these two in the same circle?'

lessons.title: What is Union-Find? (Start here)
lessons.body: Union-Find (also called Disjoint Set Union, DSU) answers one question fast: 'are these two items in the same group?' — while groups keep merging over time. Every item points to a parent; following parents leads to the group's root, its representative. Two items are in the same group exactly when they share a root. union(a, b) merges two groups by pointing one root at the other.

lessons.title: The full class — path compression + union by rank
lessons.body: Two optimisations make Union-Find nearly O(1) per operation. Path compression: while finding the root, re-point every node you pass directly at the root, flattening the tree for next time. Union by rank: always attach the shorter tree under the taller one, so trees stay shallow. Together, operations cost O(α(n)) — effectively constant.

lessons.title: Pattern: cycle detection and counting components
lessons.body: union() returning false means 'these two were ALREADY connected' — so adding this edge would close a cycle. That one insight solves Redundant Connection and drives Kruskal's minimum-spanning-tree algorithm (skip edges that would form a cycle). Counting components is just as neat: start with n components and subtract one on every successful union.

easy.title: Number of Provinces
easy.body: Count friend groups from an adjacency matrix.
easy.hint: Union every connected pair; count distinct roots.

medium.title: Redundant Connection
medium.body: Find the edge that turns a tree into a cycle.
medium.hint: First edge whose union() returns false.

hard.title: Accounts Merge
hard.body: Merge accounts that share any email address.
hard.hint: Union accounts via shared emails; group emails by root.

quiz.q: union(a, b) returns false (a and b already share a root). What did you just discover?
opts: This edge would close a cycle
quiz.why: Both endpoints already connected + a new edge between them = a cycle. Core of Redundant Connection & Kruskal.

quiz.q: Path compression does what during find(x)?
opts: Re-points every node on the path directly at the root
quiz.why: The tree flattens as you query it — future finds become near-O(1).

quiz.q: Counting connected components with DSU: start at n and…
quiz.why: Each true merge fuses two groups into one; failed unions (already connected) don't count.

cheatsheet.oneLiner: Merge groups + 'same group?' in near-O(1).
cheatsheet.useWhen: Edges arrive over time; connectivity queries; cycle detection; Kruskal MST.
cheatsheet.pattern: union() returns false → edge closes a cycle. Components = n − successful unions.
cheatsheet.gotcha: Without path compression + rank it degrades to O(n) chains. It can merge but never split.

roadmap.focus: Arrays, Strings, Two Pointers, Sliding Window

items: Merge sort / quick sort from scratch

drills.q: Find the indices of two numbers in an UNSORTED array that add up to a target, in one pass.
drills.why: Two pointers need sorted data. With unsorted input, store value→index in a hash map and check for (target − current) as you scan. O(n).

drills.q: Find a pair summing to a target in a SORTED array, using O(1) extra space.
drills.why: Sorted input + no extra space = converging two pointers. Sum too small → move left up; too big → move right down. O(n).

drills.q: Find the length of the longest substring without repeating characters.
drills.why: 'Longest contiguous run with a constraint' is the sliding-window signature: expand right, shrink left when the constraint breaks.

drills.q: Continuously receive numbers from a stream; at any moment return the K-th largest seen so far.
drills.why: Keep a min-heap capped at K items — its root is always the K-th largest. Each insert is O(log K), far better than re-sorting.

drills.q: Find the shortest path out of a maze (grid of walls and open cells), where every step costs the same.
drills.why: BFS explores level by level, so the first time you reach the exit is via the fewest steps. Dijkstra is only needed when steps have different costs.

drills.q: Count how many 'islands' of connected 1s exist in a binary grid.
drills.why: For each unvisited land cell, flood-fill (DFS or BFS) marks the whole island; count how many fills you start. O(rows × cols).

drills.q: Given course prerequisites, determine whether all courses can be finished.
drills.why: Prerequisites form a directed graph. All courses are finishable iff there is no cycle — Kahn's BFS or DFS coloring detects it.

drills.q: Implement search-box autocomplete: given a prefix, return all dictionary words starting with it.
drills.why: A trie walks the prefix in O(prefix length), then DFS collects every word below that node. Hash maps can't query by prefix.

drills.q: Find the minimum element in a rotated sorted array in better than O(n).
drills.why: The array is two sorted halves. Compare mid with the right end to decide which half holds the minimum — halve the range each step. O(log n).

drills.q: Generate every possible subset (power set) of a list of distinct numbers.
drills.why: 'Enumerate everything' = backtracking: choose → recurse → un-choose. 2ⁿ subsets exist, so exponential output is unavoidable.

drills.q: Find the fewest coins needed to make a given amount from arbitrary coin denominations.
drills.signal: min/max ways to reach a total + arbitrary denominations
drills.why: Greedy fails for coin sets like {1,3,4} making 6. DP builds dp[amount] = 1 + min(dp[amount − coin]) — optimal for any coin system.

drills.q: A robber can't rob two adjacent houses. Maximize the total loot.
drills.signal: max value + each choice constrains the next
drills.why: Overlapping subproblems: best(i) = max(best(i−1), best(i−2) + money[i]). Classic 1-D DP; greedy can lock you out of better options.

drills.q: Given a list of time intervals, merge all that overlap.
drills.why: Sort by start time, then sweep: if the current start ≤ previous end, they overlap — extend the previous end. O(n log n).

drills.q: Given meeting intervals, find the minimum number of conference rooms needed.
drills.why: Sort by start; a min-heap holds end times of ongoing meetings. Reuse a room if the earliest-ending meeting is done; heap size peak = rooms needed.

drills.q: Detect whether a linked list contains a cycle, using O(1) extra space.
drills.why: A hash set works but costs O(n) space. Floyd's tortoise & hare: fast moves 2, slow moves 1 — they meet iff there's a cycle.

drills.q: Check if a string of brackets '({[]})' is balanced.
drills.why: Nesting is LIFO: push openers, pop on each closer and check the match. Counting alone fails on ' )( ' — order matters.

drills.q: For each element in an array, find the next element to its right that is greater than it.
drills.why: Keep a stack of indices with decreasing values. When a bigger value arrives, it answers everything popped. Each index pushed/popped once → O(n).

drills.q: Numbers arrive one by one; report the median after every arrival.
drills.why: A max-heap keeps the lower half, a min-heap the upper half; keep sizes balanced and the median is at the tops. O(log n) per insert.

drills.q: People become friends over time; repeatedly answer 'are X and Y in the same friend circle?'
drills.why: Union-Find merges groups and answers 'same group?' in near-O(1) amortized. Re-running BFS per query would be O(V+E) each time.

drills.q: Versions 1…n; a hidden version is 'first bad' and all after it are bad. Find it with fewest checks.
drills.why: The predicate flips exactly once — binary search the boundary in O(log n). Any 'first X where condition holds' has this shape.

drills.q: Return the K most frequent words in a large document.
opts: Hash Map count + Heap of size K
drills.why: Count with a hash map (O(n)), then keep a min-heap of size K by frequency — O(n log K), cheaper than fully sorting the counts.

drills.q: Find the maximum of every contiguous window of size k in an array, in O(n) total.
drills.signal: max/min of each sliding window + O(n)
drills.why: A deque keeps indices with decreasing values; front is the window max. Push/pop each index once → O(n). A heap gives O(n log k).

drills.q: Transform 'hit' into 'cog', changing one letter at a time, every step a dictionary word — fewest steps.
drills.why: Each word is a node, one-letter changes are edges — all equal cost. Fewest transformations = shortest unweighted path = BFS.

drills.q: Find the contiguous subarray with the largest sum.
drills.signal: max sum of a contiguous subarray (negatives allowed)
drills.why: Kadane's: extend the running sum, or restart at the current element if the sum went negative. Sliding window fails when negatives are present.

drills.q: Answer many queries: 'what is the sum of elements between index i and j?' on a static array.
drills.signal: many range-sum queries + array doesn't change
drills.why: Precompute prefix[i] = sum of the first i items once (O(n)); every range sum is prefix[j+1] − prefix[i], O(1) per query.

drills.q: Given n dice rolls needed to reach exactly a target sum, count the number of ways.
drills.signal: count the number of WAYS to reach a target
drills.why: 'Count ways' + overlapping subproblems = DP: ways(dice, target) = Σ ways(dice−1, target−face). Plain backtracking recomputes the same states exponentially.
